newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - Looser NZ fiscal policy a safe bet.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Looser NZ fiscal policy a safe bet.

text.p: By David Plank, chief economist at Bankers Trust NZ.
AUCKLAND, Sept 19 - Last Friday the Reserve Bank of New Zealand released its six-monthly assessment of the New Zealand economy.
It provided a gloomier outlook for the economy over the next two years than the Treasury's pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update released the previous day.

While this was not a surprise, the downward revision to the RBNZ's estimate of potential growth and the likelihood of fiscal slippage after the election have led us to review our track for monetary policy over the rest of 1996 and the first half of
We still think that an easing in monetary conditions beginning in the fourth quarter of 1996 and continuing into the first quarter of 1997 is possible.

However, the easing may not go as far as previously thought. Our forecast is now for 90-day bank bills to reach 8.0 percent by March 1997, compared with 7.50 percent previously. Our March 1997 forecast for the Trade-Weighted Index is unchanged at 64.0. These forecasts are conditional on a centre-right government continuing after the election. If there is a change in government, then the mix and level of monetary conditions could
differ substantially.

As the market had generally expected, the RBNZ concluded that the outlook for the economy did not yet allow an easing in monetary conditions. However, some "encouraging preliminary signs" had emerged and the "easing in due course" scenario was still in place.
Indeed, to reflect this and to avoid forecasting zero inflation in 1998, the RBNZ built a slight easing into its projections via a constant nominal exchange rate assumption.
This was a change from the constant real exchange rate assumption used in the last few years, which requires an appreciating nominal exchange rate.
The bank's outlook should in no way be seen as a forecast.
The assumed mix of monetary conditions (90-day bank bills at 10 percent and the TWI at 65) is unrealistic.
With the market "assured" that interest rates will not fall for some time, the currency is unlikely to be anywhere near the level assumed.
In which case, why adopt the assumption?
The bank has done so to avoid projecting inflation falling to zero in 1998. This allows it to keep its rhetoric on inflation tough and so keep interest rates high.
With considerable uncertainty existing about the post-election policy mix there is some justification for this.
The market has reacted to the statement by tightening conditions through a higher exchange rate. This seems likely to continue, unless political uncertainty drives the currency lower.
The bank's projections show inflation falling rapidly in 1997. By December 1997, the RBNZ projects annual underlying inflation to be below 1.0 percent.
If monetary policy does not act on the economy with a lag, then why does this outlook not yet allow an easing in conditions?
The bank argues that while the medium-term inflation outlook is very favourable, "conclusive evidence has not (yet) emerged" that inflation pressures are past their peak.

In common with other forecasters, the RBNZ is reluctant to place undue weight on its medium-term projections. The usual uncertainty about the medium-term outlook is compounded by the uncertain election outcome.
The RBNZ's projections (and the Treasury's for that matter) are based on the assumption that government expenditure and taxation follows current policy.
Thus, while the second round of tax cuts and previously announced expenditure decisions are built into the forecasts there is no further fiscal slippage.

In our view one of the safe bets to make about the post-election environment is that fiscal policy will be loosened. By this we mean that there will be extra spending over and above what has already been committed.
This will have an impact on monetary policy.
This extra expenditure could be significant. New Zealand First have indicated they will spend an additional NZ$1.6 billion per year.
Labour's policy promises add up to more than this (at the time of writing the details of Labour's overall programme were not available).

While there is an offset from the tax increases on high income earners planned by Labour and a larger offset from the elimination of the second round of tax-cuts, the overall fiscal stimulus for Labour's package would be significant.
The Alliance's expenditure plans are massive, with its 1996 Alternative Budget indicating that expenditure would be some 20 percent higher in 1997/98 (excluding finance costs) than National's.
The Alliance would also increase capital expenditure.

The tax increases planned by the Alliance would provide an offset to the increase in expenditure. Our assessment is that the Alliance's fiscal policy will be more inflationary than current policy settings.

A National-dominated government is also likely to increase spending. We think spending by such a government would increase by at least $750 million in 1997/98, on top of the new spending already in expenditure baselines.
A loosening in fiscal policy is not itself a "bad thing".
Indeed, building up ever larger surpluses is probably undesirable from an economic point of view.

However, in the short to medium-term, a loosening of the fiscal stance will have implications for monetary policy. We have already seen this in the Reserve Bank's response to the government's tax cuts.
Expenditure increases of the levels discussed above will require a reaction from the RBNZ. This will be so even if the target for inflation is widened from the present 0-2 percent band.

We think this is one of the key reasons why the RBNZ is not yet willing to ease monetary policy. Its medium term projections may need to be revised considerably following the election to take into account any changes in fiscal policy.
Depending on the election outcome it is possible that fiscal policy will be eased by an amount that rules out any short-term easing in monetary policy.

The reaction of the RBNZ to easier fiscal policy may create some political tensions with the monetary policy framework. In our view, tinkering with the framework in an attempt to somehow change the trade-offs inherent in macroeconomic policy would be
shortsighted.
Uncertainty about the future stance of fiscal policy will keep the RBNZ nervous about the medium-term inflation outlook for some time yet.
This, coupled with uncertainty as to whether house prices have really turned the corner, should make the bank anxious about any sizeable fall in interest rates from current levels.
Having said this, with the currency so strong there is room for short-term interest rates to fall below the 10 percent level.

Bankers Trust's monetary conditions index (MCI) indicates that with the TWI at 66, 90-day bank bills could be around 9.25 percent without taking overall monetary conditions below the level assumed by the Reserve Bank.
However, given the RBNZ's focus on house prices the pain threshold for interest rates may be a bit higher at say 9.50 percent.

Also of interest is where the upper-limit (the point where conditions become too tight) for the TWI lies. With bank bills of around 10 percent, our MCI would imply an upper-limit for the TWI of perhaps 66.7.
If bank bills rally to around say 9.80 percent, then the threshold for the TWI moves higher to somewhere around 67.0.
These are "rules of thumb" rather than precise limits.
Over the course of this year the RBNZ has proved to be insensitive about conditions being near the top of its technical "comfort zone".
With the bank still perceiving the near-term inflation risks to be on the upside this seems likely to continue for some time yet.

The day before the release of the RBNZ's projections, the Treasury released its own forecasts of the economy and the fiscal position. The Treasury's growth forecast were considerably higher than the RBNZ's.

In the year to March 1997, Treasury is forecasting growth of 3.2 percent. In the following year, growth is expected to accelerate to 3.6 percent. In comparison, the RBNZ's figures are 2.0 percent and 2.6 percent respectively.
Again, it is important to consider the technical assumptions made in the construction of the forecasts.
The Treasury explicitly assumes an easing in monetary policy beginning in the December quarter of this year and continuing into the March quarter of 1997.
The boost to growth this provides, coupled with an upsurge in confidence after the election explains much of the difference with the RBNZ's forecasts for the year to March 1997.

From this point the Treasury's higher estimate of non-inflationary growth (almost 3.5 percent versus the RBNZ's estimate of 2.7 percent) leads to a more favourable output-inflation trade-off over time.

Not surprisingly, The Treasury's more rosy outlook for growth translates into a much stronger fiscal position that that forecast by the RBNZ. On a "no change in fiscal policy" basis, the Treasury expects surpluses of $2.9 billion in 1996/97 and $3.4 billion in 1997/98. The equivalent RBNZ projections are $2.2 billion and $1.9 billion.
The differences show the significant impact that growth has on the fiscal position.
They also point to possible problems in the future if the RBNZ's view of the economy's potential is the correct one.
While Treasury's surpluses are large enough to accommodate the spending plans of NZ First and Labour and still leave something of a buffer, the RBNZ's are not.
It is interesting to consider whether the commitment of political parties to run surpluses is more flexible than their commitment to increase spending.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
